title: Saving for gifts before December
description: December is expensive partly because it is predictable. Twelve small monthly deposits turn the gift season from a squeeze into a plan.

body.heading: Do the December maths in January
paragraphs: Think back to last December and estimate honestly what gifts, travel, food, and celebrations cost. Suppose the total was $480. Divided by twelve, that is $40 a month — noticeable, but manageable in a way that $480 in one month is not.
If January feels too soon to think about December, remember that is exactly the point. The people who find December calm are the ones who started while it still felt far away.

body.heading: A pot with a season
paragraphs: Open a gifts-and-celebrations pot and feed it monthly. Include birthdays across the year in the same pot if you like; celebrations are one category of life, and the pot does not care which one it funds.

Buying early has a second benefit: you can shop when prices are fair rather than when shelves are picked over and delivery is desperate. A list kept through the year — ideas noted when people mention things — makes the money go further too.

body.heading: Protect the pot's job
paragraphs: The pot is not spare money in November when something shiny appears. It already belongs to December's people. Keeping that boundary is what makes the season feel generous instead of anxious.
If December still overshoots the pot, note the real figure for next year's maths rather than feeling the plan failed. The pot's first year is an estimate; its second year is a measurement.

takeaway: Estimate last December's cost, divide by twelve, and save it monthly — the most predictable expensive month of the year deserves a plan, not a surprise.
